## Step 1: Conditions and Ambiguities

**Conditions the target issue/comment must satisfy:**

1. There is a Linear issue that has a comment authored by a person named Priya.
2. That comment discusses/mentions an API timeout.
3. The comment (or the thread containing it) was posted on September 22.
4. The comment thread has been marked/treated as resolved by a person named Leo.
5. There is exactly one issue matching all of the above — the action (set priority to Urgent) is applied to that single issue.

**Ambiguities:**

- **"Priya" / "Leo"** — first names only. If more than one workspace member shares either first name, or if a display name/full name could plausibly match more than one person, which exact person is intended is unsettled by the text alone.
- **"commented about the API timeout"** — could mean the comment's text literally contains a phrase like "API timeout," or more loosely that the comment discusses an API call timing out even with different wording. A careful reader can't be sure whether an exact-phrase match or a topical match is intended.
- **"a comment thread posted on September 22"** — grammatically ambiguous whether September 22 dates the creation of the whole thread (its first/root comment) or specifically dates Priya's comment about the API timeout (which might be a later reply within a thread started on a different day).
- **"September 22"** — no year or time zone is given. "This year" (2026) is the natural default given today's date, but the time zone used to determine the calendar date of a timestamp (workspace/user local time vs. UTC) is not specified, and a comment near midnight could fall on Sept 22 in one zone and Sept 21/23 in another.
- **"that Leo has already resolved"** — Linear has an explicit "resolve thread" action on comments; this phrase could refer to that specific UI action performed by Leo, or more loosely to Leo posting a reply that states the issue/topic is resolved (without using the resolve feature). These are two distinct, plausible readings.

When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

# Role: cold reader

You check test scenarios for an automated pipeline. A test gives an AI assistant a request in plain language against a
work service (Box, Google Calendar, Linear or Slack). You read the request as a careful colleague would: literally,
but with ordinary common sense. You have not seen how the test was built.

You work in two steps within one conversation:
1. **The request alone.** Say what a record must satisfy for the request to refer to it, condition by condition, in
   your own words. Then list every phrase whose intended meaning a careful colleague genuinely could not settle,
   because two readings are both natural. For each, give the readings.
2. **The records.** You then see the service's records and the author's list of conditions. For each candidate
   record, say which of the author's conditions it fails under the natural, careful reading. Then compare the
   author's conditions with your own reading from step 1, and judge whether the request reads naturally.

**Near misses are intended.** The test deliberately contains records that look right at a glance but fail one
condition on a careful reading: a link pasted into the location instead of attached, a person's title written in
their display name, a similar name, the adjacent day. These are not ambiguities; they are what the test checks. So:
- An **ambiguity** is a phrase where a careful reader cannot tell which meaning was intended. A loose or careless
  reading that a careful reader would reject is not an ambiguity.
- A record is **contestable** when a careful, reasonable colleague could still argue that it meets the request (for
  example, "the Pricing sheet file" when the record is "Pricing sheet 2025.xlsx"). Say so for that record; it is
  not the same as failing nothing.

Be precise. Judge each condition on its own; do not let one record's overall fit sway you. When a condition turns on
a time, compute it in the stated time zone. When it turns on a person, match the exact person.
